newsitem.title: USA: Slower growth expected for U.S. economy in '97, '98.
newsitem.headline: Slower growth expected for U.S. economy in '97, '98.

text.p: The U.S. economy should weaken slightly over the next two years, steering clear of recession but keeping interest rates low and inflation under control, a Reuters poll of 34 economists suggested Friday.
While none of the respondents in the quarterly survey forecast a recession, they expected slower consumer spending to moderate the nation's economic growth over the next eight quarters.
"There will be a slowing of consumption, but it won't show through too much in the first quarter," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
On average, the economists estimated gross domestic product growth will slow to a 2.1 percent rate by the end of 1997 from an expected rate of about 3.9 percent in the first quarter of this year.
GDP growth should remain near the 2.0 percent level through early 1999, those surveyed said.

So far this year the U.S. economy has showed no signs of substantial easing, as consumers take advantage of affordable interest rates to buy big-ticket items such as cars and furniture. If the economy continues to grow this year, it will be the seventh consecutive year of economic expansion.
The Commerce Department will release its first estimate of first-quarter 1997 GDP Wednesday.
The agency said GDP grew at an annualized rate of 3.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, up from a 2.1-percent rate in the prior quarter.
Meanwhile, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of GDP, rose 3.4 percent on an annualized rate in the fourth quarter of last year. Third-quarter consumer spending rose 0.5 percent.
"The low-interest-rate environment and tremendous gains in the employment situation are fuelling income and consumer confidence," said Joseph Dziwura, vice president and economist at Sakura Bank Ltd.
To keep inflation at bay, the Federal Reserve in March boosted its key federal funds target rate by one-quarter of a percentage point, to 5.50 percent, its first rate hike in more than two years.
On average, economists said they expected the Fed to raise interest rates twice more this year. And the increase in interest rates is sure to tighten consumers' purse strings, analysts said.
"The (economic) drag will most likely come from interest-rate sensitive sectors of the economy," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
Further rate hikes by the Fed and continued strength in the dollar should limit gains in the core Consumer Price Index, a key measure of inflation, despite an unemployment rate below 5.5 percent.
On average, the economists projected core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, would expand 2.7 percent in 1997 and 3.0 percent in 1998.
"We do think the core is likely to drift up in 1997 with the decline in the unemployment rate," said Paul Kasriel, chief U.S. economist at Northern Trust.
But the increases expected for the foreseeable future should be "benign," Kasriel said.
Once the Treasury bond market senses that future inflation may not be as problematic as it has recently feared, long-term interest rates should ease, the survey showed.
On Friday the benchmark 30-year bond yielded 7.14 percent, but the economists forecast that it should dip below 7.0 percent by the end of 1997 and should be closer to 6.75 percent by end-1998.
That would mean lower mortgage and credit card rates.

Each quarter, Reuters polls economists at banks, securities firms and research institutions to gather economic forecasts for the United States. Thirty-four experts in the United States and Canada participated in the April survey.
